question: What happens in the body during asphyxia?

options.A: Sudden spike in systemic blood pressure levels
options.B: Oxygen deprivation and carbon dioxide buildup
options.C: Excessive loss of body fluids and electrolytes
options.D: Infection of the lower respiratory airways

explanation: Asphyxia describes the dangerous combination of low oxygen (hypoxia) and high carbon dioxide (hypercapnia) caused by interrupted breathing. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why do body cells stop working properly so quickly when a person cannot breathe?

options.A: Blood vessels dilate and trap water inside tissues
options.B: Cells lack oxygen needed for aerobic energy production
options.C: The body temperature drops below normal operating ranges
options.D: White blood cells attack healthy internal organ tissues

explanation: Aerobic respiration requires a continuous supply of oxygen to produce cellular energy, which stops immediately when breathing ceases. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h1)

question: Which part of the brain controls the breathing reflex when oxygen levels drop?
explanation: The respiratory center located in the medulla detects high carbon dioxide levels and stimulates forceful breathing efforts. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h2)

question: What causes blood pH to drop rapidly during an episode of asphyxia?

options.A: Accumulation of carbon dioxide and lactic acid
options.B: Loss of sodium through the kidneys during filtration
options.C: Excessive production of red blood cells in bone marrow
options.D: Rapid breakdown of circulating blood proteins

explanation: Trapped carbon dioxide and anaerobic lactic acid combine to create a state of severe acidosis in the body. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is the main reason a person suffocates during a drowning incident?

options.A: Fluid filling the lungs and blocking gas exchange
options.B: Complete paralysis of peripheral skeletal muscles
options.C: Spontaneous rupture of the heart muscle walls
options.D: Sudden freezing of blood within surface vessels

explanation: Inhaled water occupies the air sacs in the lungs, preventing oxygen from crossing into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h3)

question: How does carbon monoxide poisoning cause the body to suffocate?

options.A: It causes the trachea to swell shut instantly
options.B: It triggers severe allergic reactions in the bronchioles
options.C: It destroys lung tissue through immediate chemical burns
options.D: It binds strongly to hemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport

explanation: Carbon monoxide attaches to hemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen does, starving body tissues even when the airway is fully open. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h3)

question: Which physical sign usually appears first when someone starts struggling for air?
explanation: Initial oxygen starvation causes a bluish skin discoloration and desperate, frantic attempts by the patient to draw breath. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h4)

question: Why might a patient with severe oxygen shortage start having seizures or convulsions?

options.A: Rapid accumulation of calcium in the bones
options.B: Sudden overstimulation of the digestive system
options.C: Profound oxygen deprivation affecting brain function
options.D: High levels of circulating white blood cells

explanation: Lack of oxygen to the brain disrupts normal electrical activity, which can lead to involuntary muscle spasms and seizures. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h4)

question: What is the best diagnostic test to measure a patient's blood oxygen and acid-base balance?
explanation: An arterial blood gas (ABG) test provides exact measurements of oxygen, carbon dioxide, and blood pH during emergencies. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h5)

question: Why might a finger pulse oximeter give inaccurate readings during severe asphyxia?

options.A: Peripheral vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the fingers
options.B: The device only measures blood pressure instead of oxygen
options.C: Carbon dioxide interferes with the light sensor directly
options.D: High fever causes the sensor screen to malfunction

explanation: When the body is in distress, it redirects blood to vital core organs, leaving fingers with weak pulse signals that confuse the sensor. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h5)

question: What concentration of oxygen should nurses deliver during an emergency resuscitation for asphyxia?
explanation: High-flow supplemental oxygen ensures maximum saturation of any functional hemoglobin left in the blood during resuscitation. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h6)

question: When would a doctor perform an emergency surgical cricothyroidotomy on a patient?

options.A: When upper airway obstruction cannot be bypassed by standard methods
options.B: As the first routine step for any patient experiencing dyspnea
options.C: Only after confirming normal arterial blood gas test results
options.D: Whenever the patient develops a mild upper respiratory infection

explanation: Cutting through the cricothyroid membrane is an emergency lifesaving measure used when standard intubation or foreign body removal fails. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h6)

question: Which organ system suffers the fastest and most severe damage from lack of oxygen?
explanation: Brain tissue has very high energy needs and stores virtually no extra energy, making it extremely vulnerable to oxygen cuts. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h7)

question: What is a common lung complication in patients who survive near-drowning?
explanation: Water in the lungs and the resulting inflammation damage the tiny air sacs, often triggering acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h7)

question: Which tool should the nurse use to monitor brain recovery in a post-asphyxial patient?
explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale checks eye opening, speech, and physical movement to track a patient's level of consciousness over time. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h8)

question: Why is teaching home safety to families an important part of patient recovery care?

options.A: It replaces the need for professional nursing follow-up visits
options.B: It guarantees the patient will never take medications again
options.C: It helps prevent future recurrence of airway obstruction accidents
options.D: It eliminates the financial costs of hospital readmissions

explanation: Educating families about choking hazards and home risks makes future episodes of suffocation much less likely to happen. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T8#GNS123_U3_T8_h8)
